scenario: A reviewer approves hundreds of AI proposals a day. Approval rates are near 100 percent and review times are very short.
question: What does that suggest?

options.text: The loop may have become a ritual. Redesign the review: focused screens, safe defaults, realistic volume and seeded test cases.
The AI is nearly perfect, so reduce review.
Add more reviewers to approve faster.

why: Warning signs of rubber-stamping include near-100 percent approval with very short review times. Adding reviewers does not fix a design problem.

scenario: An AI step can tag tickets, draft summaries, send standard customer emails and release payments.
question: How do you decide which need approval?

options.text: Classify each action by reversibility, blast radius, external visibility and regulatory exposure, and set a default pattern per action. Payments need human approval always.
Pick one policy for the whole workflow.

why: A single process contains actions of very different weight. Writing down the matrix gives you a documented answer when someone asks why an action does or does not need approval.

scenario: A reviewer sees an AI proposal. The model is unsure about two fields but the review screen shows the whole document.
question: What is the better design?

options.text: Show the decision, evidence and reason together, highlight the uncertain fields and make the default 'needs more information' instead of 'approve'.
Show only the final answer so the reviewer is not distracted.
Ask the reviewer to proofread the whole document carefully.

why: Reviewers do far better with a focused question than an open-ended 'please check'. The safe choice should be the easy one.

scenario: You want to know if your reviewers really catch errors.
question: What is the most honest test?

options.text: Seed known test cases with planted problems, explain why this is done, and measure the catch rate.
Ask reviewers whether they feel careful.
Count how many items each reviewer clears per hour.

why: Seeded cases show whether review is real. Measuring speed alone rewards speed, not quality.

scenario: An AI action has run well under full approval for months. The team wants less friction.
question: How do you loosen control safely?

options.text: Move to the lightest control that is still safe, based on evidence: shadow, full approval, exception-based review, then monitored autonomy, with graduation and demotion criteria set in advance.
Remove approvals everywhere at once and see what happens.
Keep full approval forever to be safe.

why: Approval for everything forever is not the goal. Predefined demotion criteria mean controls tighten again automatically if quality slips.
